arrival.note: A BOUND FROM THE PAPER, NOT AN ARRIVAL. The corpus first prints this person at the Democrat of 26 November 1833, column 31, so they are in the town's paper by 1833-11-26 and at no stated time before it; nothing reached says when they came. Last printed 1833-11-26.

arrival_year.note: DRAWN, NOT READ. The household's arrival block holds a BOUND — somebody was here by 1833-11-26 and no source says when they came — so the year is drawn from the arrival years the known layer records, truncated at that bound and renormalised. It says what a household of this bound most likely was, and nothing whatever about this household.

origin.note: DRAWN FROM A SURVIVORSHIP SAMPLE. No source says where this household came from. The region is drawn from the birthplaces of the seventy Old Settlers who registered an arrival at or before 1835 — a self-selected roll set down forty-four years later that over-represents the men who stayed and prospered, as the town model's own open questions say. It is the only origin distribution this project holds and this value is drawn from it, not measured.

last_dated_appearance.note: NO SIGHTING, SO THE LEG IS A SOURCE'S SPAN. The card holds no dated reading of this person at or before the scene date; the date here is the far end of what a cited source COVERS, which the role's own note calls the source's bound and not the man's. Read from `roles[] (source_span)` as `1833-11/1835-08`, which reaches 1835-08-31 — a window that covers 1835-07-01 itself, so it pins no last sighting before the day and cannot be read as one. THE FIELD IS THE EVIDENCE UNDER THE VERDICT, not a new claim: nothing here moves the presence off `uncertain`, and T-1159 and T-1172 classify this household by this date instead of reading it out of the prose (T-1144 acceptance 9).

present_on_scene_date.note: THE CORPUS STOPS BEFORE THE SCENE DATE. Last printed 1833-11-26, at the Democrat of 26 November 1833, column 31, and nothing reached either follows this person to 1 July 1835 or says they left. A documented resident whose whereabouts on one day are unknown is `uncertain` here rather than dropped: that is the same distinction index.json draws for Jeremiah Porter, and it is a finding rather than a gap.

dated_bounds.identity_rule: WALKER JAMES matches James Walker: the forename names James Walker of the 4 people of this surname, and the forename agrees in full.
dated_bounds.note: A DATED APPEARANCE IN A LAND REGISTER, AND NOTHING FURTHER. The Residence column reads UNKNOWN, which places this purchaser nowhere: the register did not record where the purchaser lived. A purchase is a TRANSACTION and not a RESIDENCE, so `here_by` is null: nothing in this register says this person was at Chicago on or before any day. Its only column that speaks to residence reads a county, a state, or UNKNOWN, and never a town. THE IDENTITY IS INFERRED AND THE REGISTER IS NOT. The date, the tract and the purchase number are the register's own, indexed by the Illinois State Archives from the land offices' sale volumes. What no source states is that the purchaser is the person on this card: data/research/land_sales/resident_crosswalk.json joins WALKER JAMES to this card on a name, upheld under T-1034, on the ground “forename_agrees”. A bound whose subject is inferred is an inferred bound. No grade moves here and the identity is neither reopened nor hardened.

appearance_bounds.source_title: Fifth census of the United States, 1830 — the division headed 'Peoria & Putnam Counties & Territory attached'
appearance_bounds.identity_rule: Surname and given name both agree between the 1830 reading 'James Walker' and the town person 'James Walker' in household hh_walker_james. The 1830 line is carried as EARLIER EVIDENCE for that person and grades nothing on its own.
appearance_bounds.note: A BOUND ON PRESENCE IN A DISTRICT, AND NOT AT CHICAGO. The division is headed 'Peoria & Putnam Counties & Territory attached' and the schedule never writes the word Chicago — the Fox River and Du Page settlements are inside it — so this row bounds presence in that district in the summer of 1830 and puts no body in the town, which is why `here_by` is null. The record's own note says it first: 'Presence in that district in the summer of 1830; not a Chicago residence, and never an 1835 one'. Under the evidence ladder ratified 2026-09-03 a source EARLIER than the scene date corroborates and dates and never promotes, and a source LATER than it does not promote either. THE IDENTITY IS INFERRED AND THE PAGE IS NOT: the leaf is read scan_verified off the federal schedule, and what no source states is that the head of family on it is the person on this card. data/research/census_1830/resident_crosswalk.json joins them on a name agreement and says in terms that it grades nothing on its own. No grade moves here and the identity is neither reopened nor hardened.

persons.note: A DOCUMENTED PERSON, AND NOTHING ELSE IS CLAIMED. The papers name 'James Walker, J. P.' and give the trade; they do not say where this household lived, who else was in it, or when it came. So the record around this person carries nothing but the person: no dwelling, no division, no family, each written as unattested in its own block rather than filled in from the shape of the rest of the town. Cited at the Democrat of 26 November 1833, column 31. THE TOWN NEVER INVENTED A ROOF FOR THIS TRADE. The occupation census raised reconstructed households for the trades a town of 3,265 people needed and could not document; `justice_of_the_peace` was not one of them, which is why this person could only ever be ADDED and never seated on an existing record — data/research/newspapers/register_1835.json calls it `new_resident` for exactly that reason. No figure is drawn (docs/LIBERTIES.md L1). READ THROUGH A TRANSCRIPTION, not a scan: the owner's ruling of 2026-08-28 grades a transcription-mediated reading as documented, and the source record for the run states that standard and its limits. A scan read that confirms or corrects the name upgrades this entry. THE FEDERAL LAND TRACT SALES — A PURCHASE, AND NEVER A RESIDENCE. The Illinois State Archives' Public Domain Land Tract Sales register enters this person 2 times, as “WALKER JAMES”, 1830-10-04: 2 lots in the platted town — lot 4 of block 10 in the town the register codes CHIOT (L4BL10CHIOT, as printed); lot 4 of block 19 in the town the register codes CHIOT (L4BL19CHIOT, as printed), 0.00 acres stated in all, for $56.00 (ls1528, ls1529). THE REGISTER'S OWN RESIDENCE COLUMN READS UNKNOWN on these rows: a county, a state or nothing, and never a town, which is why a purchase here places nobody. THE TOWN LOTS ARE THE PLAT ITSELF, AND THEY ARE NOT ACRES: Cook County's register describes them by lot and block in a platted town and gives them no section, no township and no acreage at all, so they add nothing to the acre figure above and $56.00 to the money. This project does not expand the register's town codes, so which addition a lot stands in is carried as the code and not as a name. It is still a purchase and it still places nobody. A purchase and nothing more. It dates and places a transaction; it proposes no residence, and under the ratified ladder it corroborates rather than mints. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: WALKER JAMES matches James Walker: the forename names James Walker of the 4 people of this surname, and the forename agrees in full. (data/research/land_sales/resident_crosswalk.json). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a land entry is a second source about a TRANSACTION rather than about who was living at Chicago on 1 July 1835 — a man may buy a quarter-section he never sees. T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict.

roles.note: THE BOUND IS THE SOURCE'S, NOT THE MAN'S. This role is carried by the card's 1835 occupation block and is dated by what the cited source or sources are ABOUT, which is why `precision` can be no better than the span they cover. The span reaches 1835, so this role stands in the scene-date view. The printing the trade was read off is not on the card and is fetched by T-1254.

merge_ruling.for_merge: F against W is one letter to a distance, and the initial J agrees with both James Walker the justice of the peace. 'Falker' is set nowhere at all in the deposited corpus, which is the profile of a mis-read surname rather than a family.
merge_ruling.against_merge: THE INITIAL J HAS TWO RIVALS AND THE SAME COLUMN PRINTS THEM BOTH. The Democrat of 26 November 1833, column 31, sets 'Walker, James' and 'Walker, Jeremiah' — two Walkers of this town whose forenames both begin with J, in one printing. An initial with two rivals attaches to neither: R2. The town holds four Walker cards in all (walker_george_e, walker_george_h, walker_james, walker_jeremiah) and the surname is set 396 times in the corpus, while 'J. B. Falker' is one post-office reading of 1 July 1835 (#c006) with a middle initial B that neither Walker carries. Refused by a ratified rule; no ballot needed.

basis.note: Drawn from the 1840 Chicago schedule's column 'free white males 40 under 50', one of its male bands, conditioned on `named_on_a_roll_15_and_over` because the person is named in their own right on any other roll this layer was minted from - a letter list, a subscription, a court docket, a trade notice - or carries a role, a trade, a marriage or a parenthood.

replaceable_by.match: a source that states this person's age, their birth year, or an interval either can be read out of

age_band.note: AN AGE BAND, NEVER A YEAR. No source this project holds bears on when this person was born, so the band is drawn from the only committed sex by age distribution the project has - the 1840 Chicago schedule, five years after the scene and a town twice the size - seeded by this person's own id ('walker_james:age_bands_1840'). AND THE CONDITIONING IS THE MODEL'S, NOT A SOURCE'S: that a roll naming a person in their own right names somebody 15 or over. The 1840 schedule counts a child as a tally inside a household and never as a correspondent; 15 rather than 20 because an apprentice or a journeyman stands on a trade roll. No source states this rule. No exact year is written, because a year drawn from a decadal band would read as a record of a birth.

sex_basis.note: A FORENAME THAT STANDS IN ONE SEX'S NAMING ONLY. 'James' is read as male because 2 persons in this layer whose sex a source records bear it (couch_james, kinzie_james), and it stands in the irish and yankee male forename pool of this town's own attested naming. Nothing about this person is recorded; the name is the whole of the reasoning, and the table that licenses it — data/research/residents/forename_sex.json — refuses a name its own evidence splits, refuses Jean, Marion, Leslie and Francis by name, and refuses an initial outright.

research_note: MINTED FROM THE NEWSPAPER REGISTER (T-0376), AND THE HOUSEHOLD IS A CONTAINER RATHER THAN AN ARGUMENT. Every other record in this dataset argues for a household — a family the sources count, or a trade the town demonstrably needed. This one argues for a PERSON: the Democrat and the American name James Walker as a justice of the peace at Chicago 1 time(s), and this reconstruction did not hold them. `data/residents/` has no way to carry a person except inside a household, so one was written around them and told to claim nothing: one member, no dwelling, no division, no origin, no arrival beyond the bound the paper sets. Reading a family, a house or a quarter of town into this record would be reading something the papers do not say. tools/mint_documented_residents.py derives the whole minted set and prints every candidate it refused, with the reason.
